VANAD: Named-Vessel-Aware Aneurysm Detection and Segmentation in TOF-MRA

Anonymous WACV Algorithms Track submission Paper ID *****
Abstract

Intracranial aneurysms are searched for in time-of-flight MR angiography, where the target may occupy a few dozen voxels on a thin, tortuous arterial tree and where the normal bifurcations that must be dismissed resemble, in intensity alone, the lesions that must be found. Existing methods supply vascular priors almost always as a binary notion of vesselness, which cannot express which artery a voxel belongs to and therefore cannot state how a location deviates from the normal calibre of its own segment. The facts that define an aneurysm are relational — wider than its neighbourhood, adjacent to a junction, absent contralaterally. From a frozen thirteen-class arterial parcellation we compute those comparisons in closed form as a local radius residual, a within-segment radius z-score and a junction proximity. To ensure the parcellation is used rather than merely available, the labels define the regions over which features are pooled into per-territory tokens and the support onto which the token-derived modulation is scattered back, so the pathway cannot be bypassed. The two resulting heads are supervised per arterial territory and per voxel. We evaluate on 2,132 pooled TOF-MRA studies and an independent cohort of 272, against six published methods retrained under one protocol. The proposed model attains a lesion-level F1 of 0.734 on the internal test cohort and 0.719 on the independent external cohort, at 0.064 and 0.092 false positives per case.

1Introduction

Unruptured intracranial aneurysms are found in an estimated 3.2% of adults without comorbidity [25], and although most never rupture, aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage remains among the most lethal forms of stroke. Time-of-flight MR angiography is the primary non-invasive modality for finding and following these lesions, because it resolves the intracranial arteries without contrast or ionising radiation. The task is adversarial in a specific way: the object of interest is a small outpouching on a bright, branching tubular structure, and the distractors are the normal branch points of that same structure. Both are locally bright and blob-like, and what separates them is not local appearance but a comparison against the vessel that carries them.

The literature poses this task either as detection or as segmentation and treats the two as interchangeable. Clinically they are not. Detection must establish that a lesion is present and where on the arterial tree it sits, because the parent vessel determines rupture risk and the choice between observation and intervention [9, 23, 26]. Segmentation turns a detected lesion into a measurable one, since diameter, neck width, dome-to-neck ratio and interval growth are read off the boundary. These are two scales at which the same output must be correct, so we supervise the network at both: a territory-level objective asking, for each labelled arterial segment, whether it carries a lesion, and a voxel-level objective constraining the mask.

Anatomical priors have long been used to make this search tractable, but the dominant formulation biases the model with a binary notion of vesselness — a vessel region of interest [8], a Frangi-type channel [20], a cascaded coarse vessel segmentation [16], or an auxiliary vessel task [10]. These establish that telling the network where the arteries are helps, but none can express which artery a voxel belongs to, leaving the network to rediscover from intensity alone the segment identity and calibre norms a radiologist uses [6]. Handing a network one vesselness value per voxel supplies one side of a comparison and leaves the comparison to be learned. We compute the result instead. From a thirteen-class parcellation produced by a frozen network we derive a local radius residual against the narrowest neighbouring vessel, a radius expressed as a z-score within the segment the voxel belongs to, and a proximity to the nearest junction between two segments. None is computable from a binary vessel mask, and none from a local receptive field over intensity, however deep.

Supplying such information is not the same as using it: a gated fusion of dense anatomical features can be satisfied by generic context, and a side input competing inside a shared stem can be ignored once the main pathway lowers the loss on its own. We therefore make the labels the definition of the pooling regions rather than an extra channel: features are pooled per territory into tokens, the tokens receive the territory-level supervision directly, and they are written back onto the voxel grid through a modulation whose support is again the territory masks. Perturbing the labels therefore changes the computation itself rather than a learned input weight.

We make four contributions. First, we formulate aneurysm analysis as a two-scale supervision problem, a territory-level objective combined with a voxel-level one in a single network. Second, we replace the binary vascular prior with a thirteen-class parcellation and introduce label-conditional geometric descriptors not computable from a binary mask. Third, we inject anatomy through territory-defined pooling and territory-scattered modulation rather than an input channel, with a label-shuffling negative control. Fourth, we assemble a pooled multi-source TOF-MRA benchmark with an explicit eligibility audit, derive a trainable reference standard from heterogeneous annotations, and report external validation against six published methods under one protocol.

2Related Work

Aneurysm analysis in TOF-MRA. The task has been addressed both as voxel segmentation [11] and as lesion detection [17], evaluated with different instruments: overlap and surface distances on one side, sensitivity at a false-positive budget on the other. Because cohorts, reference standards and matching rules differ across studies, published numbers are not comparable, so we retrain every comparator on one benchmark under one protocol.

Vascular priors as auxiliary information. Almost all existing formulations tell the network where the vessels are with a binary notion of vesselness: patches drawn inside a vessel region of interest [8]; a Frangi-type map as an input channel and inside a decoder attention block [20]; a multi-scale Hessian filter defining the region within which segmentation is performed [18]; a cascaded coarse vessel segmentation [16]; or an auxiliary task against class imbalance [10]. Beyond aneurysms, anatomy has been injected as pseudo-label input channels with transformer-guided fusion [15]. None of these can express segment identity. We change both the content of the prior, from binary to thirteen labels, and the route by which it enters, from a channel that can be down-weighted to the definition of pooling regions and of a modulation support.

Backbones and the reliability of comparisons. A recent systematic re-evaluation found that much reported progress in volumetric segmentation does not survive rigorous validation and that residual-encoder U-Nets remain state of the art [13]; our backbone is one, and its plain form is one of our baselines. Repeated training under different seeds also produces a spread that can exceed the differences between architectures [1], so each configuration is trained under several seeds and a difference smaller than that spread is reported as not decidable.

3Method

3.1Overview

The model carries two streams over a shared three-dimensional residual-encoder U-Net topology. A frozen stream reads anatomy: a thirteen-class arterial parcellation network trained beforehand on vessel labels and never updated by the aneurysm objective. A trainable stream of identical architecture predicts the aneurysm. The anatomical stream is consumed in three ways — per-scale decoder features that gate the lesion decoder, closed-form geometric channels, and territory masks that define pooling regions and modulation support — and the network terminates in two heads supervised at two scales (Figure 1). Freezing the anatomical stream makes the anatomical representation identical across every configuration we compare, so differences are attributable to how anatomy is used rather than to how well it happened to be learned; the frozen network is held in evaluation mode and loaded strictly.

3.2Reference standard

The four sources of our internal cohort annotate aneurysms in three incompatible ways: one marks each lesion by position only, a second gives a sphere of the reported diameter, and only the third gives a traced contour. A sphere stamped on a saccular aneurysm covers parent artery and parenchyma and, where the sac is eccentric, omits part of the lesion, so a model trained on the mixture reproduces a systematic error. We therefore express every annotation as a ball that always contains the annotation it replaces, then refine it against the image: the flow core is detected inside the ball as the largest connected region above a fixed normalised intensity, and the sac boundary is recovered by a watershed on the gradient magnitude with the eroded core as foreground marker and a shell just outside the ball as background, so the label is cut at the intensity edge rather than at a fixed quantile. A lesion with too small a core to be perfused keeps its ball, because there is no image evidence on which to cut. Every threshold is a single global constant fitted once against expert traces by grouped cross-validation, with nothing tuned per case or per source.

3.3The anatomical stream and its three products

The frozen network is a residual-encoder U-Net predicting background plus thirteen arterial classes, supervised by VAN13-MRA, a named 13-class vessel label resource that extends a public brain TOF-MRA cohort with pseudo-rich named-vessel segmentations for 1,168 studies, released with case-level quality metadata and a clinician-audited subset of 200 studies [2]. Its vocabulary is comparable in granularity to the thirteen-class circle-of-Willis vocabulary used by public challenge resources [27], and we use the labels as distributed.

The fold used to train the frozen stream excludes our aneurysm test split entirely: 795 of its studies come from our training split and 119 from our validation split, while none comes from our test split. The anatomical stream is therefore never optimised on an image in the internal test set we report, and never on aneurysm labels at any point. Three products are taken from it: per-scale decoder features condition the fusion inside the lesion decoder; full-resolution class logits, softmaxed over the thirteen foreground classes, give soft territory masks; and closed-form operators applied under no gradient yield the geometric channels.

3.4Geometric channels

Six channels are concatenated and given to the geometry pathway, none with trainable parameters. Three are image-derived shape descriptors: a vesselness response from the Hessian eigenvalues, a shape index, and a curvedness. Three are conditional on the parcellation. The radius residual is the local vessel thickness minus the smallest thickness in a neighbourhood restricted to vessel voxels, encoding how much wider a location is than the narrowest vessel adjacent to it. The within-segment radius z-score standardises thickness by the mean and standard deviation of the segment the voxel belongs to, encoding how unusual the calibre is for that particular artery. The junction proximity is an exponentially decaying distance to the nearest point at which two different arterial labels meet. Two choices follow from sliding-window inference: we use a local thickness field rather than a centreline radius, because skeletonisation depends on global topology and changes at tile boundaries; and we take a local minimum rather than a smoothed average as the reference calibre, because averaging mixes the dilated segment’s own value into its baseline, while the minimum imports the parent-vessel value unchanged so that a uniform tube yields exactly zero.

3.5Injection: three routes, one resolution

All three injections occur at a single decoder resolution, laid out stage by stage in Figure 2. Co-locating them means the contribution of each can be attributed, and they form a ladder in which each stage requires the previous one. The first route is a dedicated geometry encoder: the six channels pass through a small strided convolutional encoder and are added into the decoder feature map through a zero-initialised pointwise projection. It is intentionally shallow, because its purpose is not capacity but a private path along which gradient can reach the geometric input; fed through a shared stem, this pathway lost the competition with the main input and contributed nothing.

The second route is the territory tokens. The soft masks are resampled to the feature grid and used to take a mask-weighted average of the concatenated decoder and geometry features, one vector per territory. A second, axially dilated variant of each mask is pooled alongside, because an aneurysm grows outside the lumen and pooling strictly inside the mask omits the sac; the dilation is axial only, since the grid is anisotropic. The vectors are embedded and related by a small transformer encoder, and an auxiliary head predicts per territory whether it carries a lesion. The third route writes the tokens back: a linear map produces a scale and a shift per territory, scattered onto the grid by the same masks and applied after the last decoder stage. This is what makes the label information non-bypassable, since changing the labels changes the modulation and its support; it too is zero-initialised.

3.6Objective

The total loss is the sum of a voxel term — class-weighted cross-entropy with an ignore label plus a focal Tversky-type region term — and a masked binary cross-entropy on the per-territory logits, weighted by a single coefficient. Three properties of the territory term are structural. Its positive weighting is derived from the batch rather than fixed, because few of the thirteen territories are typically positive. Cases whose lesion cannot be attributed to any territory are excluded from this term only, since teaching the model that every territory is negative would inject a label error. And the logits are softly clamped, because a hard clamp has zero gradient outside its range, so a strongly weighted positive voxel that leaves it could never return. The voxel loss is a fixed control axis and is not re-tuned per configuration.

3.7Inference

Inference is sliding-window with Gaussian importance weighting. Turning a probability map into candidates requires a decision rule anchored to a seed, so post-processing can never invent a candidate the model did not produce. Components are formed at a low threshold, only those reaching the operating threshold are retained, the survivors are dilated, and a component is discarded if too small a fraction of its voxels lies inside the parcellation. Selection must precede dilation, since otherwise a sub-threshold neighbour could attach to a survivor. The pipeline transforms the probability map rather than a mask, each survivor painted with its own maximum probability and dilated greyscale, so one pass produces a map correct at every threshold, and the full FROC curve can therefore be recomputed after post-processing. The threshold is re-selected on the validation split whenever ensemble size or post-processing changes.

4Experiments

4.1Datasets

Our internal cohort pools four publicly released TOF-MRA collections, listed in Table 1: the aneurysm-detection release of a recent large challenge [19], whose thirteen-segment taxonomy is the one our parcellation uses; a single-institution cohort with spherical weak labels [7, 8]; a clinical database with traced segmentations [4, 5]; and a public collection of healthy volunteers from three centres and three scanners [14], used as aneurysm-negative controls. Eligibility was assessed once per study with mutually exclusive criteria: releases without a clinician segmentation on a TOF-MRA series; non-MR-angiographic and non-time-of-flight series, excluded by a full visual audit confirmed against acquisition parameters; blank, corrupt and conversion-failed volumes; and byte-identical duplicates. Of 5,268 released studies, 2,132 entered, 753 aneurysm-positive, spanning four scanner vendors and both common field strengths, split case-wise into 1,489 training, 222 validation and 421 test studies. The validation split is used only to select thresholds and post-processing parameters.

4.2Implementation

Training used AdamW with a cosine-annealed learning rate and short warm-up, in mixed precision, with patch sampling constrained so each batch contains at least one aneurysm-positive patch, and deep supervision over the upper decoder levels. The modules introduced by our method received a larger learning-rate multiplier than the warm-started backbone. All runs used deterministic kernels and every configuration was trained under several seeds. Exact constants and checkpoints are in the supplementary material.

4.3Baselines

We compare against six published methods spanning the three families of Section 2. Four are general-purpose three-dimensional segmentation networks without an anatomical prior: a self-configuring pipeline [12], its residual-encoder variant [13], a ConvNeXt-style scaled convolutional network [21], and an efficient hybrid-transformer network [22]; the residual-encoder variant shares our backbone family, so comparing against it separates the anatomical exchange from the backbone. The fifth supplies a Frangi vesselness map both as input and inside a decoder attention block [20], the closest competitor since it is exactly the binary formulation our parcellation replaces; the sixth uses a multi-scale Hessian filter to define the vessel region within which segmentation is performed [18]. All six were retrained on our cohort with the same split, reference standard, preprocessing grid and threshold discipline; published numbers are not quoted, because cohorts and matching rules differ and one comparator was developed on one of our sources.

4.4Metrics and statistical analysis

We report eight quantities: lesion-level F1, sensitivity, precision, false positives per case, voxel Dice at the locked threshold, voxel Dice at the oracle threshold, and the sensitivities attainable within false-positive budgets of 0.10 and 0.25 per case. A lesion counts as detected when its centre of mass falls inside a predicted connected component, each lesion is matched at most once, and a component containing no ground-truth centre is a false positive. The two budgeted sensitivities are read off the FROC curve without interpolation and left blank when a curve does not reach the budget, since clamping favours models whose curves stop early. We do not summarise the FROC curve by an area. Over the interval from zero to eight false positives per case the fraction of the curve that has to be extrapolated because the curve stops early varies from 30.8 to 87.1 per cent between seeds of the same model, and reaches 92.3 per cent for the five-arm logit ensemble, so an area would not be measuring the same thing across runs. The curve is therefore shown as a figure only.

The operating threshold is the one that maximises lesion-level F1 on the validation split, and it is then locked for the internal test and external cohorts, so the operating point is a property of the screening decision rather than of the metric it is scored with. Voxel Dice is measured at a second threshold, selected on the same split by maximising voxel Dice and locked in the same way, because a threshold chosen for detection is not the one at which overlap is read. We also report voxel Dice at the threshold that maximises it on the evaluated cohort itself; that value is an upper bound and is never used as a result. Because the reference standard differs in kind between the two cohorts, overlap metrics are compared only within a cohort. Because repeated training of one configuration produces a spread of the same order as the differences between variants, we report the between-seed standard deviation and mark any smaller difference as not decidable.

5Results

Table 2 reports both cohorts at the operating threshold of 0.40 locked on the validation split. The reported model is a five-arm logit ensemble. On the internal test cohort the proposed model reaches a lesion-level F1 of 0.7340, from a sensitivity of 0.6770 and a precision of 0.8015 at 0.0641 false positives per case. On the external cohort it reaches 0.7193, from a sensitivity of 0.6286 and a precision of 0.8408 at 0.0919 false positives per case. The two figures are close at the lesion level, and the difference between them is largely a trade of sensitivity for precision rather than a change in overall detection quality. We do not combine the metrics into a composite score.

Voxel Dice is 0.3658 on the internal cohort and 0.4089 on the external one. As stated in Section 4.4 these two values are not comparable with one another: the internal reference standard is derived from coarse annotations by the refinement of Section 3.2, so the internal figure is overlap against a target whose extent was reconstructed rather than drawn, whereas every external label is traced. Neither figure should be read as a delineation accuracy comparable across the two cohorts.

Read off the FROC curve at fixed budgets, sensitivity is 0.7019 at both 0.10 and 0.25 false positives per case internally, and 0.6286 and 0.6429 externally. Because the locked operating point already sits at 0.0641 and 0.0919 false positives per case, below the tighter budget in both cohorts, relaxing to 0.10 adds 0.0249 sensitivity internally and nothing externally, while widening to 0.25 adds nothing further internally and 0.0143 externally. The internal curve is therefore flat across the interval the two budgets span, and no value is extrapolated beyond the point each curve attains.

To complete · author note

Baseline comparison. Table 2 currently carries the proposed model only; the six retrained comparators are still running. Once they finish, read each metric separately across both cohorts and state which differences exceed the between-seed spread reported in this section.

Repeated training under different seeds produces a spread that is not a single number: it depends on the metric, the cohort, and whether post-processing is applied. Without post-processing the lesion-level F1 spread is 0.016 internally and 0.031 externally, and a difference smaller than that is not decidable. Post-processing narrows it as well as raising the score — the lesion F1 standard deviation falls from 0.0160 to 0.0115 internally and from 0.0313 to 0.0108 externally, and the operating Dice from 0.0156 to 0.0056 internally. The mechanism is measurable: the gap between the oracle threshold and the locked threshold, averaged over five seeds, collapses to +0.0008 internally and +0.0003 externally after post-processing, from +0.0276 and +0.1656 without it, where externally the oracle threshold sits at the grid floor of 0.01 in every seed. Post-processing removes a degree of freedom in the threshold. The least stable quantity is the external false-positive rate without post-processing, whose standard deviation is 0.0895 over a range of 0.180 to 0.368, and the threshold the validation split selects itself scatters between 0.3 and 0.7 across seeds.

The supplementary material carries two component contrasts, and they differ in what they settle. The loss and transfer-scope comparison is complete at three seeds across four arms: Focal Tversky++ and Dice move detection and overlap in opposite directions, and transferring encoder and decoder rather than the encoder alone separates the arms externally while leaving them not decidable internally. The injection ladder is also reported there, at equal budget, but we state its reach here rather than in an appendix. Of its four steps only the FiLM scatter produced a gain beyond the seed spread, and only on the internal test cohort; the geometry encoder alone and the territory pooling alone were not decidable, and externally no step of the ladder exceeded the control. The label-shuffling negative control is a single seed and did not separate from the control externally, so it does not support the claim it was designed to test. The comparison in Table 2 is against published methods and its differences are not attributed to any single component.

6Discussion and Limitations

Our comparison establishes how the model performs relative to six published methods trained and evaluated under one protocol. It is not designed to attribute that performance to a single component, and we say so explicitly; the injection ladder in the supplementary material isolates the routes at equal budget, and of its four steps only the FiLM scatter separated from the seed spread, on the internal cohort alone. Two structural properties hold independent of the numbers. The label-conditional channels compute quantities a local receptive field over intensity cannot compute at all, since a within-segment calibre z-score requires knowing the segment. And both injection routes are zero-initialised, so the model at initialisation is numerically identical to one without them; whatever behaviour they produce is learned rather than imposed.

Several limitations follow from the data and the design. Most positive cases in the internal cohort were annotated as coarse spheres or positions and the target was derived from them by the refinement of Section 3.2, which changes lesion volume substantially, so overlap values are not comparable with values computed against ball-style labels nor across cohorts. The anatomical stream is a model rather than an oracle, supervised by generated rather than drawn labels, so it inherits whatever systematic error that generation carries; and it is a prediction, so the territory objective is undefined for lesions outside every predicted segment and a lesion whose parent vessel it misses cannot be helped by any route. The external cohort is a challenge release whose largest centre comes from the same institution as one of our internal sources; we removed the declared re-distributions and verified that no further same-patient overlap is detectable, but that is a similarity test rather than identity resolution. Finally, all results are TOF-MRA, and because the model consumes a lateralised parcellation it does not transfer unchanged to modalities in which that parcellation is unavailable.

Two directions follow from the structure. The anatomical stream is frozen, so any improvement in parcellation quality propagates to all three routes without retraining the lesion model; and the territory head already produces a per-segment prediction, which is what a clinical report names.

7Conclusion

We asked what changes when the anatomical prior given to an aneurysm model stops being binary. The facts that distinguish an aneurysm from a normal bifurcation are relational, and once a thirteen-class arterial parcellation is available those relations — deviation from the calibre of the same segment, proximity to a junction — can be computed in closed form and supplied directly rather than left for the network to infer from intensity. And supplying anatomy is not the same as using it: by letting the labels define the pooling regions and the support of the modulation, the pathway becomes one the model cannot bypass. Supervising the resulting heads per arterial territory and per voxel matches the two questions the clinical task actually asks. On the pooled benchmark the resulting model reaches a lesion-level F1 of 0.734 on the internal test cohort and 0.719 on an independent multi-centre cohort, at fewer than 0.1 false positives per case.
